name: Lost-wax casting at Mehrgarh
summary: Metalworkers at Mehrgarh in Balochistan cast small copper amulets from wax models about 6,000 years ago, the oldest lost-wax casting known.
description: At Mehrgarh in Balochistan, founders modelled small wheel-shaped amulets in a wax-like material, formed a clay mould around the model, melted it out and poured in very pure copper. The shape could not have been released from a permanent mould, and photoluminescence imaging of one corroded amulet by Thoury and colleagues recovered the structure of the original casting. The paper calls the amulet 6,000 years old, shows its find area as Early Chalcolithic (end of period III, 4,500-3,600 BC) and identifies it as the oldest known lost-wax cast object.

impact.note: Lost-wax castings were ornaments and ceremonial objects made by specialist founders (reach 1) and improved on existing casting by allowing shapes no permanent mould could release (depth 1); the cited study reports that Baluchistan founders went on to cast leaded copper by the same process through the fourth and third millennia BC, and its wider claim of spread across the ancient Near East is untested, so only these direct successors are counted (generativity 1).

date.label: about 6,000 years ago (c. 4000 BCE)
date.basis: As the cited source gives it.

events.statement: Thoury and colleagues describe the Mehrgarh amulet as 6,000 years old (about 4000 BCE, counted from the present) and identify it as the oldest known artefact made by lost-wax casting.

evidence.supports: a 6,000-year-old amulet from Mehrgarh (Baluchistan, Pakistan), identified as the oldest known artefact made by lost-wax casting

earliest_record.rationale: The earliest dated evidence found for this capability in this community. No review has yet confirmed that nothing earlier exists.

unresolved.note: Compare the Mehrgarh amulets with the Nahal Mishmar hoard and the Varna gold, which are close in date, and settle whether lost-wax casting was reached separately in each; the cited paper only says Nahal Mishmar may be an independent invention.
The paper gives the amulet's age as a round 6,000 years and the find area as 4,500-3,600 BC; a stratigraphic or radiocarbon date for the amulets themselves was not found.
The paper's claim that lost-wax casting spread from Baluchistan across the ancient Near East needs a source that tests it against the Levantine evidence.

research.note: Thoury and colleagues (2016) identify the Mehrgarh amulet as the oldest known lost-wax cast artefact; they add that Nahal Mishmar in the Levant is possibly contemporaneous and may represent an independent invention. The early gold castings of Varna were not checked.
